passage: Hrithik, I saw you punch your pillow after that phone call. Let your Chandrika Bua tell you about being fifteen. I had a temper like a pressure cooker. One day my best friend Shobha laughed at my poem in front of the whole class. I came home and wrote her a letter so cruel my hand shook. I was running to the post box when my father said, "Post it tomorrow if you still want to." That evening I went up to the terrace and skipped rope till my legs burned, then poured everything into my diary. By morning the letter looked like someone else had written it. I tore it up and told Shobha, calmly, that she had hurt me. She said sorry. We are still friends, two old women now. Feelings are storms, beta. They pass.

qa.q: Where did Chandrika skip rope?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she wrote the letter?
qa.a: She felt furious and humiliated, so angry that her hand shook.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chandrika's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Waiting overnight at her father's suggestion and letting the anger out through skipping and her diary; by morning she could talk to Shobha calmly instead of sending something she would regret.

qa.q: How might Shobha have been affected if the cruel letter had been posted?
qa.a: She would have been deeply hurt, and a friendship that lasted into old age might have ended.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that big feelings pass, using exercise and writing as outlets, and waiting before sending something in anger.

passage: The night before the maths exam, rain hammered the Kochi flat and the power kept flickering. Then Mehak saw it: Thomas had posted her old mispronunciation video in the class group, with three laughing faces. Her face burned. She typed fast: "You're pathetic and everyone knows it." Her thumb hovered over send. Instead she set a timer for an hour and threw the phone onto her bed. The rain was too heavy for her usual run, so she put on loud music and danced round her room till she was breathless, then wrote everything in her notebook, ugly words included. When the timer rang, she deleted the draft and messaged Thomas privately: "That video really embarrassed me. Please take it down." Soon it was gone, with a "sorry, didn't think". She went back to her maths.

qa.q: How long did Mehak set the timer for?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she saw the video?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious; her face burned and she typed a cruel reply.

qa.q: Which of Mehak's choices prevented regret, and why?
qa.a: Waiting an hour, dancing and writing out the anger before replying, so she sent a calm, clear request instead of an insult.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt receiving the calm message instead of the insult?
qa.a: Thomas could see the hurt clearly without getting defensive, which made it easy to apologise and take the video down.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with a storm of feelings finding outlets in music, movement and writing, and waiting an hour before sending a message.

passage: Sabina saw the screenshot at 6:10 pm: her private message about her crush, forwarded by Gopika to the class group. Her face burned. In their Hyderabad flat she typed fast: "You're a snake. I hope everyone finds out what you're really like." Her thumb hovered. Then she remembered the rule she'd made after last month's fight with Ammi: one hour before sending anything angry. She put the phone in the kitchen drawer, grabbed her racquet, and smashed shuttlecocks against the colony wall until her arms ached. Then she wrote three furious pages in her notebook. At 7:15 she opened the drawer. The feeling was still there, but smaller. She deleted the draft and wrote instead: "That was private. I'm really hurt. Please delete it and tell me why." Gopika replied within a minute: "It was an accident. I'm so sorry. Deleting now."

qa.q: What time did Sabina see the screenshot?
What was Sabina feeling when she typed the first message?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious, face burning, betrayed by Gopika.

qa.q: Which steps helped Sabina manage the storm?
qa.a: Waiting an hour with the phone in a drawer, smashing shuttles, and writing in her notebook, so she could send a calm, honest message.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt receiving the calm message?
qa.a: Gopika was likely relieved and ashamed, quick to apologise and delete.

grounding: Shows a teenager letting a big feeling pass by waiting an hour and using sport and writing before sending a message, which prevents regret.

passage:
"Joseph, how was the final?"
"Don't."
"Oh. That bad?"
"I missed the penalty. In front of everyone. I'm quitting. I'm leaving the team group right now."
"Okay. Can you not do that for one hour?"
"Why?"
"Because last time you quit something at nine at night, you begged to rejoin at nine in the morning."
"That was the choir. Different."
"Is it? Go and play your guitar for a bit. Loud as you want. I'll make noodles."
"Fine. One hour."
An hour later:
"Leela Chechi? I'm not quitting. I'm still angry, though."
"You're allowed to be angry. You're just not allowed to delete things while you're boiling."
"Can I have extra noodles?"
"Already done."

qa.q: What did Joseph miss in the final?
qa.a: The penalty.

qa.q: How was Joseph feeling after the final?
qa.a: Joseph felt humiliated and angry, ready to quit and leave the team group.

qa.q: Why did waiting an hour help?
qa.a: The big feeling passed enough for Joseph to see quitting was a reaction, and playing the guitar gave the anger an outlet.

qa.q: How does Leela see Joseph's urge to quit?
qa.a: Leela sees it as the storm talking, remembering how quitting the choir at night was regretted by morning.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that a big feeling passes, using music and a one-hour wait instead of quitting in anger.

passage: When I was fourteen, my feelings came like monsoon storms: sudden, huge, gone an hour later. I'm Hafsa, and I once slammed my bedroom door so hard the latch broke, after Abbu said no to a school trip. I once sent Payal a message saying I never wanted to see her again, over a seat on the bus, and spent a week trying to fix it. What helped wasn't anyone telling me to calm down. It was noticing the pattern. My cousin said, "The feeling is real, but it isn't permanent." So I made myself a deal: when the storm comes, I wait one hour. I walk three rounds of the colony park with loud music, or I write it out in the back of my maths notebook, or I call Payal and just rant. Most of the time, after an hour, I don't want to send the message anymore. There are a lot fewer broken latches now.

qa.q: What broke when Hafsa slammed the door?
qa.a: The latch.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after sending Payal the angry message?
qa.a: Hafsa felt regretful, spending a week trying to fix it.

qa.q: What deal did Hafsa make, and why does it work?
qa.a: Waiting one hour and using walks, writing or ranting to Payal, because the feeling passes and the urge to send or slam fades.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt receiving the "never want to see you" message?
qa.a: Payal was likely hurt and shocked, over something as small as a bus seat.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that big feelings pass and using walking, writing and a trusted friend, plus a one-hour wait, to avoid regrets.

passage:
Counsellor's follow-up note, Karthik, Class 11
Two months ago Karthik came to me after smashing his phone against a wall over a group-chat fight and sending messages he deeply regretted. Today was very different. He told me that on Saturday a friend posted something hurtful about him. He felt the heat rise and typed a furious reply, then remembered our plan: wait an hour before sending anything. He went for a run round the colony instead, then played his guitar. When the hour was up, he deleted the draft, and he called the friend the next day to talk calmly. He said, 'The feeling was huge, but it passed.' I told him I was proud of him. We will meet monthly now.
Parveen

qa.q: What did Karthik do instead of sending the reply?
qa.a: He went for a run round the colony, then played his guitar.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when the friend posted something hurtful?
qa.a: He felt a rush of anger, with heat rising, and typed a furious reply.

qa.q: Which strategy helped Karthik, and why?
qa.a: Waiting an hour before sending anything, with a run and music as outlets, let the big feeling pass so he could talk calmly.

qa.q: How might the friend have experienced Karthik's calm call?
qa.a: The friend may have felt relieved and more willing to talk than if a furious message had arrived.

grounding: A teenager learns that big feelings pass, uses running and music as outlets, and waits before sending a message.
